question: Which part of the nail is responsible for making new nail cells?
explanation: Think of the nail matrix as the factory floor! It contains active cells that constantly push older cells forward to form the hard nail you see. [learn more](BMP110_U5_T4#BMP110_U5_T4_h1)

question: Why does a healthy nail bed look nice and pink?

options.A: Constant friction against footwear stimulates local blood flow
options.B: Melanin deposits accumulate densely in the lower epidermal layers
options.C: The hard keratin cells themselves contain natural pink pigments
options.D: A rich network of underlying blood vessels shines through the translucent plate

explanation: Your nail plate is actually see-through (translucent). The healthy pink color you see comes from the tiny blood vessels (capillaries) running underneath! [learn more](BMP110_U5_T4#BMP110_U5_T4_h1)

question: What is the main infection control reason for keeping a client's fingernails short and clean?

options.A: To stop clients from biting their fingers out of anxiety
options.B: To make hand massages more effective during hygiene care
options.C: To prevent the accumulation and spread of pathogenic microorganisms
options.D: To speed up the overall rate of natural nail growth

explanation: Germs love to hide under long nails! Keeping them short stops microbes from spreading to food, wounds, or other people. [learn more](BMP110_U5_T4#BMP110_U5_T4_h2)

question: A confused client keeps scratching at their healing belly surgery wound. What is the best nursing action?

options.A: Restrain both arms tightly to the bed rails until the wound closes
options.B: Scold the client firmly whenever they reach toward the dressing site
options.C: Apply strong antiseptic ointment directly over the surgical incision daily
options.D: Trim and file the client's fingernails smoothly, and consider protective mittens

explanation: Short, smooth nails and gentle mittens protect the wound from accidental scratches without resorting to harsh restraints. [learn more](BMP110_U5_T4#BMP110_U5_T4_h2)

question: Which nail condition features spoon-shaped, inward-curving nails and is often linked to iron deficiency?
explanation: Koilonychia makes nails look scooped out like little spoons—a classic sign to check your client's iron levels for anemia! [learn more](BMP110_U5_T4#BMP110_U5_T4_h3)

question: What do deep ridges running straight across the nail (Beau's lines) usually tell you?

options.A: An acute local bacterial infection caused by poor hand hygiene
options.B: A permanent genetic defect inherited from one or both parents
options.C: A temporary pause in nail growth due to a past severe illness or stress
options.D: Normal physiological aging changes in individuals over sixty years

explanation: When the body goes through severe stress or illness, it hits the pause button on nail growth. As the nail grows out later, it leaves a ridge behind. [learn more](BMP110_U5_T4#BMP110_U5_T4_h3)

question: How should you trim a client's toenails to prevent painful ingrown nails?

options.A: Deeply curved into a sharp point at both outer edges
options.B: Straight across without rounding down deep into the corners
options.C: Shortened exclusively by biting or peeling off excess keratin
options.D: Filed down heavily from the top surface using a metal rasp

explanation: Always cut toenails straight across! Cutting down into the corners encourages the sharp edges to dig into the soft skin. [learn more](BMP110_U5_T4#BMP110_U5_T4_h4)

question: Why shouldn't you aggressively cut or push back the cuticles during nail care?

options.A: It makes the nail plate grow excessively fast and thick within days
options.B: It permanently stops the nail matrix from producing any future nail growth
options.C: It causes the underlying nail bed to turn completely blue due to hypoxia
options.D: It breaks the natural protective seal, predisposing the client to painful infections

explanation: The cuticle acts as a tiny security guard keeping bacteria and fungi away from the sensitive nail bed. Leave it intact! [learn more](BMP110_U5_T4#BMP110_U5_T4_h4)

question: A diabetic client with nerve changes (neuropathy) asks you to trim their thick toenails. What is the safest action?

options.A: Inspect the feet carefully, soak the nails, and refer the client to a podiatrist for safe trimming
options.B: Ignore the request because nail care is not part of standard diabetic management
options.C: Use a sharp razor blade to shave down the thickness of the toenails immediately
options.D: Tell the client to trim their own nails at home using unsterilized household scissors

explanation: Clients with diabetes and neuropathy can easily get hurt without realizing it. Letting a specialist (podiatrist) handle it is always the safest route. [learn more](BMP110_U5_T4#BMP110_U5_T4_h5)

question: Why are even minor nicks during nail care especially risky for clients with long-standing diabetes?

options.A: Their cuticles are completely absent, leaving the nail matrix exposed
options.B: Their fingernails and toenails grow at triple the normal physiological rate
options.C: Diabetic blood contains natural chemicals that dissolve surgical instruments
options.D: Impaired peripheral circulation and reduced sensation delay healing and mask pain

explanation: Poor blood flow means cuts take forever to heal, and nerve damage means the client might not even feel a developing sore. [learn more](BMP110_U5_T4#BMP110_U5_T4_h5)

question: What is the correct infection control rule for cardboard nail files (emery boards) in the clinic?

options.A: They can be reused indefinitely if soaked in plain tap water for two minutes
options.B: They must be sterilized in an autoclave along with surgical steel instruments
options.C: They should be discarded after a single use to prevent cross-contamination
options.D: They should be wiped with dry cotton wool and shared among ward patients

explanation: Emery boards are porous and cannot be properly sterilized. Always use a fresh one for each client to keep everyone safe! [learn more](BMP110_U5_T4#BMP110_U5_T4_h6)

question: Which of these details is NOT needed when charting routine nail care in a client's records?

options.A: The specific brand name of the soap used during the hand soak
options.B: The client's reaction and tolerance to the hygiene procedure
options.C: Any abnormal findings like discoloration, thickness, or inflammation
options.D: The physical condition of the nail plate and surrounding skin folds

explanation: Good nursing documentation focuses on the client's condition and how they tolerated the care—the soap brand doesn't affect clinical outcomes! [learn more](BMP110_U5_T4#BMP110_U5_T4_h6)
